description: Density of solids, liquids and gases, changes of state, and pressure in fluids and gases.
content_html:
The Particle Model of Matter

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of how their particles are arranged and how they move. In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions in a regular arrangement by strong forces between them. They vibrate about fixed points but cannot move from place to place — this explains why solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.

In a liquid, particles are close together but can slide past each other because the forces between them are weaker than in a solid. Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. In a gas, particles are far apart with negligible forces between them. They move rapidly in random directions, colliding with each other and the walls of their container. Gases fill any container and can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles.

Key Fact

In a solid, particles are in fixed positions (vibrating only). In a liquid, particles are close but can flow past each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move randomly. Gases can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles; solids and liquids cannot.

What Is Density?

Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. A dense material has a large amount of mass in a small volume. The equation is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

Where \(\rho\) is density (\(\text{kg/m}^3\) or \(\text{g/cm}^3\)), \(m\) is mass (kg or g), and \(V\) is volume (\(\text{m}^3\) or \(\text{cm}^3\)). You must be able to rearrange the equation to find mass (\(m = \rho \times V\)) or volume (\(V = \frac{m}{\rho}\)). To convert between units: \(1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\). A common exam error is failing to convert grams to kilograms before calculating in SI units.

Question: A metal cube has a mass of 216 g and a volume of \(80 \text{ cm}^3\). Calculate its density in \(\text{g/cm}^3\).

Answer: Write the equation: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Substitute: \(\rho = \frac{216}{80} = 2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3\). This is the density of aluminium. To express in SI units: \(2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 2700 \text{ kg/m}^3\).

Measuring Density (PAG P1)

To measure the density of a regular solid (such as a cuboid), measure its mass on a balance and calculate its volume using a ruler: \(V = l \times w \times h\). For a cylinder, use \(V = \pi r^2 h\). Then apply \(\rho = m/V\).

For an irregular solid (such as a pebble), use a displacement method. Fill a eureka can until water overflows at the spout. Gently lower the object into the water and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder — its volume equals the volume of the object. Alternatively, use a measuring cylinder directly: record the initial water level, submerge the object, and measure the new level. The volume of the object equals the rise in water level.

For a liquid, measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder, pour in the liquid, and measure the total mass. The liquid’s mass is the difference. Read the volume from the graduated scale at the bottom of the meniscus. Apply \(\rho = m/V\).

Key Fact

Density of a regular solid: measure mass and calculate volume using a ruler, then \(\rho = m/V\). Density of an irregular solid: measure mass on a balance, find volume by water displacement (eureka can or measuring cylinder), then apply \(\rho = m/V\). Read the measuring cylinder at the bottom of the meniscus.

Why Densities Differ

The particle model explains why densities differ between states of matter. In solids, particles are closely and regularly packed, giving high density. In liquids, particles are slightly further apart and less ordered, so density is a little lower. In gases, particles are very widely spaced, so density is dramatically lower — typically about a thousand times less than the same substance in liquid form. Crucially, mass is conserved during any change of state: the number of particles does not change, only their arrangement and spacing. When ice melts to water, the same particles are present but occupy a slightly different volume. When water boils to steam, the vast increase in volume means density falls dramatically.

An important exception is water: ice is slightly less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats. This unusual behaviour occurs because water molecules form an open lattice structure in the solid state, taking up more volume per molecule than in the liquid state.

Pressure in Fluids

Pressure in a gas arises because gas particles constantly collide with the walls of their container, exerting a force on each unit of area. In a liquid or gas (both are fluids), pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth below the surface. The qualitative reason is that a deeper column of fluid has more weight of fluid above it pressing down, increasing the force on any surface at that depth.

For Higher tier, the pressure at a depth in a fluid can be calculated using:

$$p = h \times \rho \times g$$

Where \(p\) is pressure (Pa), \(h\) is the depth of the fluid (m), \(\rho\) is the density of the fluid (\(\text{kg/m}^3\)), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth). This equation shows that pressure increases with depth (greater \(h\)), with denser fluids (greater \(\rho\)), and in stronger gravitational fields. For example, a diver at 10 m depth in sea water (density approximately \(1025 \text{ kg/m}^3\)) experiences a pressure of \(p = 10 \times 1025 \times 10 = 102{,}500 \text{ Pa}\) from the water alone, in addition to atmospheric pressure above.

Worked example: A submarine is at a depth of 200 m in sea water (\(\rho = 1025 \text{ kg/m}^3\)). Calculate the pressure due to the water at this depth. \(p = h\rho g = 200 \times 1025 \times 10 = 2{,}050{,}000 \text{ Pa}\) (or 2.05 MPa). Always state the unit — pascals (Pa) — in the final answer.

Key Fact

Pressure in a gas is caused by particles colliding with the container walls. Heating a gas at constant volume increases particle speed, so collisions become more frequent and more forceful — pressure rises. In a fluid column, pressure increases with depth.

Heating a gas at constant volume increases the kinetic energy of the particles. They move faster, collide with the container walls more frequently, and each collision exerts a greater force. Both effects increase the pressure. This is why sealed containers such as aerosol cans carry warnings about exposure to heat — the rising pressure could exceed the container’s strength and cause it to burst.
exam_tip_html: For density calculations, always show the equation, substitution and units. A very common error is failing to convert grams to kilograms (or g/cm³ to kg/m³) when working in SI units — always check before calculating. For the displacement experiment with an irregular solid, describe the procedure step-by-step: place water in cylinder, record initial level, submerge object fully, record new level, subtract to find volume. For pressure in fluids at Higher tier, make sure you include the unit — Pa (pascals) — in your final answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains the properties of solids (fixed arrangement, vibrate only), liquids (close but can flow) and gases (widely spaced, rapid random movement). Gases have the lowest density; solids the highest.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume. For regular solids, measure dimensions with a ruler; for irregular solids, use water displacement. Mass is always conserved during changes of state.
  • Pressure in a gas arises from particle collisions with container walls. In a fluid column, pressure increases with depth. At Higher tier, fluid pressure is calculated using p = hρg.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the particle arrangement in a liquid?
A) Particles in fixed positions, vibrating about those positions
B) Particles close together but able to flow past each other
C) Particles far apart, moving rapidly in random directions
D) Particles in a regular lattice with no movement
practice_questions.marks: B) Particles close together but able to flow past each other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would measure the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: Measure the mass of the stone using a balance (1). Measure the volume using water displacement — submerge the stone in a measuring cylinder of water and record the rise in water level (volume of stone = rise in level) (1). Then calculate density = mass ÷ volume. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A steel ball has a mass of 390 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation stated: ρ = m/V (1). Correct substitution: ρ = 390 ÷ 50 (1). Correct answer in g/cm³: 7.8 g/cm³ (1). Correct conversion to kg/m³: 7800 kg/m³ (1). [4 marks — common error: dividing volume by mass, or failing to convert units]

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why a gas has a much lower density than the same substance in its solid state.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a solid, particles are closely and regularly packed, so a large mass is contained in a small volume, giving high density. In a gas, the same particles are very widely spaced (large distances between them) with negligible intermolecular forces, so the same mass occupies a much larger volume, giving very low density.
Secure: Particle spacing in each state described correctly with link to density.
Developing: States particles are far apart in gas and close in solid, but no link to mass/volume/density.
Emerging: States that gases are less dense than solids with no particle model explanation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pressure inside a sealed aerosol can increases if the can is placed near a heat source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Heating the gas inside the can increases the kinetic energy of the gas particles; they move faster; collisions with the walls become more frequent and each collision exerts a greater force; the pressure inside the can therefore increases.
Secure: Faster particles and more frequent/forceful collisions described; linked to pressure increase.
Developing: States particles move faster when heated; link to pressure increase stated but not explained.
Emerging: States pressure increases when heated with no particle-level explanation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A diving bell is lowered to a depth of 40 m in sea water. The density of sea water is 1025 kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the pressure due to the sea water at this depth. Show all steps.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: p = hρg (1). Correct substitution: p = 40 × 1025 × 10 (1). Correct answer: 410 000 Pa (or 4.1 × 10⁵ Pa) (1). Correct unit stated: Pa or pascals (1). [4 marks — Higher tier question; common errors: swapping h and ρ, omitting the unit]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the correct equation for density?
Which state of matter has particles that are far apart and move rapidly in random directions?
When measuring the volume of an irregular solid by displacement, you record the _____ in water level when the object is submerged in a measuring cylinder.
During any change of state, _____ is conserved — the number of particles does not change, only their arrangement.
Match each state of matter to the correct description of particle behaviour:
right: Particles very widely spaced; rapid random movement; fills any container
Particles in fixed positions; vibrate about those positions; fixed shape and volume
Particles close together; can flow and change shape; fixed volume

flashcard_questions.q: State the equation for density including symbols and units.
flashcard_questions.a: ρ = m/V. Density in kg/m³ (or g/cm³), mass in kg (or g), volume in m³ (or cm³).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the conversion between g/cm³ and kg/m³?
How do particle arrangements differ between a solid and a gas?
flashcard_questions.a: Solids have closely, regularly packed particles vibrating in fixed positions; gases have widely spaced particles in rapid random motion.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can gases be compressed but solids cannot?
flashcard_questions.a: Gas particles are far apart with large empty spaces between them; solid particles are already in contact.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you find the volume of an irregular solid in the laboratory?
flashcard_questions.a: Submerge it in water in a measuring cylinder; the rise in water level equals the object's volume.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is mass conserved when ice melts to liquid water?
flashcard_questions.a: The same particles are present; only their arrangement changes. No particles are created or destroyed.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
flashcard_questions.a: Ice is less dense than liquid water — water molecules form an open lattice in the solid state, occupying more volume.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes the pressure of a gas inside a container?
flashcard_questions.a: Repeated collisions of gas particles with the container walls exert a force on each unit of area.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to gas pressure when the gas is heated at constant volume?
flashcard_questions.a: Pressure increases — particles move faster, collisions become more frequent and more forceful.

flashcard_questions.q: State the equation for pressure at depth in a fluid (Higher).
flashcard_questions.a: p = hρg, where h is depth (m), ρ is fluid density (kg/m³), g is gravitational field strength (N/kg).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the PAG associated with measuring the density of solids and liquids?
At what point in a measuring cylinder should you read the volume of a liquid?
flashcard_questions.a: At the bottom of the meniscus (the curved surface of the liquid).

glossary_terms.definition: A model that explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of the arrangement and movement of particles.
A measure of how much mass is packed into a given volume of a substance. Calculated as mass divided by volume, measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³.
The curved surface of a liquid in a measuring cylinder or other glass vessel, caused by surface tension. Volume is always read at the bottom of the meniscus.
The force exerted per unit area, measured in pascals (Pa). In fluids, pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth.
